newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi prince says to buy five pct of NCL.
newsitem.headline: Saudi prince says to buy five pct of NCL.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's billionaire Prince al-Waleed bin Talal said on Wednesday he has agreed to buy a five percent stake in the Norwegian Cruise Lines (NCL) worth $20 million.

A statement from the prince's office in Riyadh said he has "agreed to subscribe to new shares of Norwegian Cruise Lines Holding ASA (NCL) for an amount of $20 million equal to five percent of the enlarged capital."

"I have long held an interest in the direction being taken by the cruise industry and after spending many months researching the investment options available, I see in Norwegian Cruise Lines strong management and an excellent potential and opportunity for growth in an area which is the fastest growing in the leisure industry," the prince said.

NCL said this month it had agreed to buy the Royal Majesty cruise liner from Kvaerner ASA as part of expansion plans. NCL was formerly known as Vard ASA, which has been restructured after a debt crisis.

"The recent deal with Kvaerner ASA and now the participation by his royal highness, leaves NCL with strong shareholders and a solid balance sheet. The phase of recovery is completed and NCL can now continue expansion of the company," the statement quoted Kristian Siem, chairman of NCL, as saying.
The statement was sent to Reuters in Dubai.
In his latest international acquisition Prince al-Waleed said last week he had purchased five percent of stock in Trans World Airlines, in what his office said was a new investment trend.

Prince al-Waleed -- who turned 40 on March 7 -- controls an international portfolio that includes a bank, an investment firm, a supermarket chain, a broadcasting operation, and huge property holdings including the Fairmont and Four Seasons hotel chains.

He has helped bail out the Euro Disney theme park near Paris and Canary Wharf in London's Docklands. Earlier this year he bought Paris' luxury George V hotel. He also has stakes in U.S. banking giant Citicorp.
